title: Should You Allow Students To Wear Pajamas During Zoom Lessons
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Addressing a genuinely controversial pandemic-era question, Linsin argues teachers should hold a minimum dress standard for Zoom lessons even though students attend from home. He acknowledges the counterarguments — that parents control what's worn in their own home, that pajamas are harmless comfort — but contends that allowing pajamas sends a message that online school isn't fully real, which erodes the mental preparation needed for learning. He frames the pajama rule as a small but symbolically powerful boundary: allowing it opens a 'slippery slope' toward stuffed animals, breakfast in bed, and general disengagement, whereas holding the line protects attentiveness and classroom culture. He closes with a broader argument that low expectations, however well-intentioned, ultimately harm students by denying them the challenge needed to build genuine self-respect and perseverance — while still endorsing occasional, deliberate 'Pajama Day' as a fun exception.
points: Allowing pajamas during Zoom lessons signals that online school isn't fully real, weakening student mental preparation.
Small, seemingly frivolous dress expectations function as the foundation for larger success habits.
Permitting pajamas opens a slippery slope toward stuffed animals, breakfast in bed, and general disengagement.
A minimum dress standard measurably improves attentiveness during already-challenging Zoom lessons.
Occasional, deliberately scheduled 'Pajama Day' is a fine and fun exception to an otherwise consistent standard.
quotes: Allowing pajamas communicates to students that they’re not really in school and that expectations during Covid are lax, if they exist at all.
The smallest foundational expectations, however—those that appear frivolous at first glance but mentally prepare students for learning—are in fact incredibly powerful in the message they send.

If you allow pajamas, then here come the stuffed animals. Here come the waffles and cereal and laying in bed. It’s a slippery slope that will never end unless you create a boundary that protects their learning.
Add pajamas and the distractions and lack of commitment they can cause and it becomes next to impossible to teach effectively.
When we challenge students, on the other hand, when we set foundational standards for them, when we send the message that through hard work they can excel, they become transformed.
PS – Allowing a “Pajama Day” once a month or so is fun and I wholeheartedly endorse the practice.
